_meta: A lease granted for a duration, subject to network delay and clock skew, used to show that a holder which uses the full granted duration on its own clock can still be acting after the grantor has expired the lease and reassigned it -- two holders at once -- and that the holder must treat the lease as SHORTER than granted by a safety margin covering the delay plus the skew. A lease grants exclusive use of a resource for a duration D. The grantor starts counting when it sends the grant and will reassign the lease at grant-time D. The holder starts counting when it receives the grant, which is later by the network delay, and its own clock may run slow relative to the grantor's, so its D-timer takes extra real time to elapse. If the holder uses the full D from receipt, its stop moment in the grantor's timeline is delay + D + skew -- past the grantor's expiry at D -- so there is a window where the grantor has already given the lease to someone else while the old holder still believes it holds it, which is the same two-writers hazard a lease was meant to prevent. The fix is for the holder to use an effective lease of D minus a safety margin, where the margin is at least the maximum network delay plus the maximum clock skew, so the holder always stops before the grantor's expiry. On this fixture D is 100, the network delay is 10, the clock skew is 15, and the margin is 30: the naive holder stops at 125 (overrunning the grantor's expiry of 100 by 25 = delay + skew), while a holder using D minus 30 stops at 95, safely before 100; a margin of only 20 still overruns. The lease duration, delay, skew, and margin are the fixture; the grantor expiry, the naive and safe stop times, and the overlaps are computed. Stdlib only.
